title: Operationalisation Laboratory
summary: Three fictional constructs, each modelled as five facets, and six candidate operational definitions apiece drawn from self-report, behavioural-trace, observational and performance-based families. Ticking measures moves a live facet coverage map and a plain-language list of what each measure also records. Coverage rises as measures are added, and so does reactivity, while feasibility falls - and full coverage of a facet list is still not the construct.
learningObjectives: Explain why an operational definition is a claim about a construct rather than a translation of it.
Distinguish construct under-representation from construct-irrelevant variance and give an example of each.
Describe the reactivity and feasibility costs of getting closer to a construct.
Say what combining measures from different families buys, and what it does not.
Identify a design in which the intervention acts directly on the outcome measure.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native select, checkboxes and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend. The facet coverage map is built from HTML rather than an image: each row prints its facet name and its standing in words - not reached, partly reached, well reached - so the bar length and the fill colour are both redundant cues. Numeric summaries appear in a definition list beside the map. The map and readout are pinned to the top of the stage so they stay visible while the measure list is worked through. Every change is announced through the shell's polite live region with a full sentence, focus moves to the laboratory heading when it opens, reduced motion is honoured for the bar transition, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Operationalisation: what a measure reaches, what it misses, and what it quietly records instead
simulationNotes: Three constructs - academic engagement, stress and social connection - each modelled as five named facets, with six candidate measures apiece. Each measure carries a coverage level per facet of 0, 1 or 2, plus a reactivity and a feasibility rating on a three-point scale and a written list of what else it records. For a selected plan the facet level is the maximum across the selected measures rather than the sum, because two partial measures of one facet do not add up to a good one. Plan reactivity is the highest among the selected measures and plan feasibility the lowest, reduced one step further for each measure beyond two. The coverage percentage is arithmetic on the facet list shown above it: it is not a validity coefficient and the page says so. The facet lists are teaching simplifications and are contested for all three constructs. No published instrument, item or proprietary assessment is reproduced; measures are described generically.
